summary: Techno (Berlin, Detroit, peak-time): 128-138 BPM, a relentless 909 kick with rumble, 16th hats, off-beat open hats and an 8th ride, a rolling or acid 303 bass, almost no harmony (one stab, a Detroit string chord), change by automation; knowledge/style/techno.json is its template
body: Tempo 128-138 BPM: peak-time about 125-135, raw and deep 130-140 (hard techno faster still).

Drums: TR-909 (or harder, shorter kicks): the kick on every beat is the track's centre, with a rumble under it (the kick through a dark reverb, high-cut below 200 Hz); closed hats in 16ths skipping the kick, open hats on the off-beats, a 909 ride in 8ths dipping on 1 and 3; no house clap on 2 and 4, rather a rim, syncopated snares and clap rolls in builds.

Bass: a sine sub on the off-beat after the kick (the 'oompa'), a rolling saw or square 16th line resting on each beat, or a TB-303 acid line with the cutoff and resonance moving; low (about E0-E1), sidechained to the kick.

Harmony: barely any: one minor chord or a single stab repeated, i-VII at most; Detroit techno adds string chords and pads, Berlin and minimal less. Movement comes from slow filter, delay and reverb automation; parts enter every 16 or 32 bars.
Lead: rare; a one- or two-note riff, a bell or vocal snippet, plucks and arps, dark and often atonal, through delay and reverb.
Texture/master: dark, dense, hypnotic and gritty; the low end mono, the kick loudest, highs controlled; a little analog drive is fine.
Sources (2026-11-26): MusicRadar 'The definitive guide to producing techno' and 'Create a rumbling techno kick'; EDMProd 'How to make techno'.

Apply: pattern/four-on-the-floor on the drums, then pattern/prog-techno-characteristic-1 on the keys four bars later. For a whole style change the Team Lead's restyle uses knowledge/style/techno.json instead.

drums.about: the drum track (a kit); leave out if there isn't one

keys.about: a chordal part (keys, pad); leave out if there isn't one

key.about: the project's key; leave out to estimate it from the notes
